check: After the next 10 SKILL.md writes, count hook blocks (exit 2) vs skill_lint --strict failures in CI. Hook blocks > 0 and CI ERROR failures == 0 supports it.
claim: Moving skill_lint from CI-only to a PreToolUse hook catches at least one frontmatter or naming ERROR at write time that CI would otherwise have surfaced a commit later. If ten SKILL.md edits pass with zero hook blocks, the hook is ceremony and should be reverted to CI-only.

check: skill_lint --strict stays clean, and over the next 5 authoring sessions no session needs a second attempt because the wrong skill loaded.
claim: Merging author-skill and session-to-skill removes a routing ambiguity rather than just renaming one. Expect skill-craft to be invoked for both authoring and distilling without the user naming a mode, and expect no new overlap finding between skill-craft and any other skill.

check: Count red CI runs on dev over the next 10 merges to dev.
claim: Running CI on dev rather than main-only catches at least one failure on dev before it reaches main within the next 10 merges. If every dev run is green and main never regressed anyway, the extra CI is cost without signal.

check: py -3.11 -m pytest -q collects and passes; the new syntax-floor test enumerates every shipped script and reports how many failed ast.parse at feature_version=(3,9) before the fix.
claim: A mechanical 3.9-syntax guard plus a CI Python matrix will catch version-floor breakage that the OS matrix alone never could; I expect it to find at least one further 3.12-only construct beyond site.py:384 in the currently shipped scripts.

evidence: First half RIGHT: 3.11 went from cannot-collect to 785 passing, and the OS matrix could never have shown it (all three CI jobs pinned 3.12). Second half WRONG as stated: there was exactly ONE further 3.12-only construct, not more - the whole repo had a single one. But a second floor violation of a different kind did exist, 'import tomllib' at module scope (3.11 stdlib, not syntax), which the prediction did not anticipate because it assumed the problem was syntactic. The most useful outcome is that the CHECK I specified was invalid: ast.parse at feature_version=(3,9) reports the pre-fix file as CLEAN, because PEP 701 is a tokenizer change and feature_version only gates grammar. I had written down a measurement instrument that cannot measure the thing. The working guard needed three passes (tokenize, feature_version, AST import scan) plus a real-interpreter CI matrix.

check: Read the python-floor matrix results on the PR into dev: four jobs (3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.13). Record which interpreters failed and on what — a SyntaxError means python_floor.py missed something static and must be extended; a runtime TypeError/AttributeError means the static checker is working as designed and the gap is inherent to static checking.
claim: The new python-floor CI job will FAIL on Python 3.9 and/or 3.10 on its first run, because python_floor.py checks syntax and stdlib imports but cannot see runtime API usage (dict | merge, zip(strict=), 3.10-only kwargs). I grepped for the common ones and found none, but a grep is not an interpreter. I put this at roughly 40 percent. If it passes on all four, the 3.9+ promise is proven across its full declared range for the first time; if it fails, the gate caught on its first real outing exactly the class of defect it was built for, and the fix is a decision (patch the calls, or raise the floor to 3.11 and say so in the README) rather than a scramble.

evidence: 3.9 FAILED on first run; 3.10, 3.11 and 3.13 passed. Predicted '3.9 and/or 3.10' at ~40 percent - right, and right about which end of the range. But the MECHANISM was wrong in an instructive way. I predicted a runtime API failure in shipped code (dict | merge, zip(strict=)). Shipped code was fine: every other test collected and passed on 3.9, so the repo does honour its declared floor. What failed was my own test, asserting that --floor 3.10 ACCEPTS a match statement - which is false when the host is 3.9, because ast.parse feature_version can only make the parser stricter, never grant it grammar the host lacks. It is not a version simulator. That is the THIRD distinct way this one API misled me in a single session (the other two: PEP 701 is a tokenizer change so feature_version misses it entirely; and tomllib is not a syntax error at all). All three are now pinned by tests. Net: the matrix earned its place on its first run, catching a real defect that no local interpreter I had could show.

check: git clone --no-hardlinks . <tmp>/fresh && run check.py --repo on both the working copy and <tmp>/fresh; diff the archive-candidate finding sets. Pre-fix: fresh clone yields zero archive findings while the working copy yields some. Post-fix: the two sets are identical.
claim: Replacing mtime with git committer date at all four archive-rule sites makes cms archive findings clone-stable: a fresh clone of hephaestus and this working copy will report an identical set of archive-candidate findings. Today they disagree, because a clone resets every mtime to checkout time and every doc reads as 0 days old.

check: Count dirs matching hephaestus-*-state-* in %TEMP%, run 'python -m pytest -q' three times, count again. Pre-fix the count rises by 6; post-fix it is unchanged.
claim: Guarding the mkdtemp calls behind an is-it-already-set check and adding pytest_unconfigure teardown reduces the per-pytest-process temp-dir leak from 2 dirs to 0. The 468 stray dirs already in %TEMP% are historical and will not grow.

evidence: Measured directly. Pre-fix, three pytest runs took the stray-dir count from 245 to 248 for each of the two prefixes (+2 per process, exactly as predicted). Post-fix, three FULL suite runs left it at 251/251 - delta 0. Predicted 2 -> 0; observed 2 -> 0. The historical dirs (490 across both prefixes at the time of writing, higher than the 468 in the handoff because the leak was still running) did not grow. Caveat on scope, not on the verdict: teardown removes only dirs the process created, so a caller-supplied CMS_STATE_DIR is never touched, and that is pinned by a test rather than left to the docstring.

Mechanism RIGHT, empirical claim WRONG, and the check I wrote down was invalid on the repo I named it against. The clone-stability property is real and demonstrated: tests/test_doc_age.py::test_a_fresh_clone_agrees_with_the_original builds a repo with a 200-day-old and a 3-day-old committed plan, clones it, and asserts both report an IDENTICAL finding set - one finding, the old one. That test fails under the mtime implementation, which is what makes it worth having. But the claim's second sentence, 'Today they disagree', was simply false about hephaestus, and I could have known before recording it: hephaestus contains ZERO files matching ARCHIVE_PATTERNS, so the rule never fires here at all. Working copy and fresh clone both reported 0 archive findings before the fix and both report 0 after. Running the recorded check verbatim on the named repo yields 0 == 0 pre- and post-fix - it cannot distinguish a working implementation from a broken one. This is the third time in this ledger that the specified instrument, rather than the claim, was the defective part (see adr-003-decompose and adr-003-ci-floor-matrix, both of which turned on ast.parse feature_version not measuring what I assumed). The transferable lesson is narrower than 'check your instrument': before recording a check, RUN it against the unfixed tree and confirm it currently FAILS. A check that passes pre-fix is not a check. Thirty seconds would have caught this one.
